analysis.investment_thesis: Honasa is a D2C digital beauty brand trading at 70x P/E with ROE of only 6.39% — a grossly overpriced business with no demonstrated ability to compound capital. Volatile earnings, declining profits year-on-year (₹111 Cr → ₹73 Cr), and promoter holding below 36% make this fundamentally unsuitable for a long-term value portfolio.
key_strengths: Low D/E of 0.11 — balance sheet is clean post-IPO recapitalization
High gross margins of 69.5% indicate strong brand pricing power in personal care
Revenue has scaled from ₹460 Cr to ₹2,067 Cr in 4 years, proving consumer demand exists
key_risks: ROE of 6.39% and ROCE of 8.04% — capital is being destroyed, not compounded; well below my 15% minimum
Promoter holding of only 35.54% — far below my 55% threshold; low skin-in-the-game is a governance concern
Business model entirely dependent on performance marketing and D2C channels — no durable moat, easily disrupted by larger FMCG players
red_flags: Net profit declining: ₹111 Cr (FY24) → ₹73 Cr (FY25) despite revenue still growing — margin compression is accelerating
Pre-IPO borrowings of ₹1,954 Cr against only ₹303 Cr of assets signals the company ran on convertible debt for years — not a quality business history
P/E of 70.5x and EV/EBITDA of 70x for a business earning 6% ROE is irrational pricing
EBITDA collapsed from ₹166 Cr (FY24) to ₹129 Cr (FY25) — no earnings consistency whatsoever
No dividend history — zero return to shareholders despite being listed
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From my perspective, Honasa fails almost every filter I use. The numbers that matter most — ROE at 6.39%, ROCE at 8.04% — tell me this business earns less than what a fixed deposit would return on the capital it employs. I built DMart by obsessing over every rupee of return on capital deployed. A consumer brand with 69% gross margins and only 6% ROE means the money is being burned on marketing, celebrity endorsements, and building multiple brand identities simultaneously. That is not a business; that is a vanity project funded by public market capital. Revenue growth of 45% CAGR sounds impressive until you see profits moving backwards from ₹111 Cr to ₹73 Cr in FY25.

The promoter holding of 35.54% is deeply concerning — when founders hold so little of their own business, I question their conviction. I prefer promoters with over 55%, ideally 65-70%, who are aligned with long-term value creation. The pre-IPO capital structure — ₹1,954 Cr in borrowings against ₹303 Cr of assets in FY21 — reveals a company that was burning cash and surviving on convertible instruments, not building a real business. The IPO cleaned the balance sheet, but it did not fix the underlying economics. At 70x P/E with decelerating revenue (₹1,920 Cr → ₹2,067 Cr, just 7.7% growth last year) and falling profits, the market is pricing in a future this company has not earned the right to promise.
